This report presents highlights and some stats to the sentiment analysis modelling using LSTM. 

# The IMDB dataset 

A quick look at the dataset. This is a standard IMDB dataset often used for tutorials.
```{python}
import os
import sys
#setting the directory
os.chdir("../..")
sys.path.append(os.getcwd())

from great_tables import GT, style, loc
from sentiment_analysis.load_imdb_data import load_imdb_data_into_df

df_imdb = load_imdb_data_into_df().head(5)
gt_imdb = GT(df_imdb)
(
  gt_imdb.tab_header(
  title="IMDB Review vs. Sentiment",
  subtitle= "The top 5 reviews in the dataset"
)
.cols_label(
  review = "Review Text",
  sentiment = "Sentiment Label"
)
.cols_align(align="left")
.cols_width(review="700px", sentiment="200px")
# Style 1: Make the main Title look bold, prominent, and dark blue
.tab_style(
        style=style.text(weight="bold", size="28px", color="#1a365d"),
        locations=loc.title()
    )
# Style 2: Give the column headers a sleek grey background with uppercase text
.tab_style(
        style=[
            style.fill(color="#f7fafc"),
            style.text(weight="bold", color="#4a5568", transform="uppercase", size="24px")
        ],
        locations=loc.column_header()
    )
    # Style 3: Highlight rows to distinguish Positive vs Negative reviews cleanly
    # (Applies custom text coloring depending on the row data value)
.tab_style(
        style=style.text(color="#2f855a", weight="bold"), # Deep Green
        locations=loc.body(columns="sentiment", rows=lambda df: df["sentiment"] == "positive")
  )
.tab_style(
        style=style.text(color="#c53030", weight="bold"), # Deep Red
        locations=loc.body(columns="sentiment", rows=lambda df: df["sentiment"] == "negative")
)
   # 1. Strong thick line directly underneath the column header titles
.tab_style(
        style=style.borders(sides="bottom", color="#2d3748", weight="2px", style="solid"),
        locations=loc.column_header()
    )
    # 2. Clean horizontal grid lines between every row inside the table body
.tab_style(
        style=style.borders(sides="bottom", color="#e2e8f0", weight="1px", style="solid"),
        locations=loc.body()
    )
    # 3. Solid, dark closing border at the very bottom of the table data grid
.tab_style(
        style=style.borders(sides="bottom", color="#2d3748", weight="2px", style="solid"),
        locations=loc.body(rows=[4])
    )
)
```
# The Dataset Characteristics
```{python}
from sentiment_analysis.load_imdb_data import load_imdb_data_into_df, train_test_val_set
import pandas as pd

df_imdb = load_imdb_data_into_df()
x_train, x_val, x_test, y_train, y_val, y_test = train_test_val_set(df=df_imdb)

dataset_charecteristics = {
    "Total number of reviews": len(df_imdb),
    "Training set(X_train)": f"{len(x_train)}",
    "Testing set(X_test)": f"{len(x_test)}",
    "Validation set(X_val)": f"{len(x_val)}"
                              }

df_dataset_characteristics = pd.DataFrame.from_dict(dataset_charecteristics, orient = "index", columns=["Total"]).reset_index()
```

# Vocabulary Characteristics

## Token length characteristics

Descriptive stats of review column

```{python}
from sentiment_analysis.pre_process_and_tokenize import preprocess_string

reviews_data = df_imdb['review']
review_token_length = [len(preprocess_string(review).split()) for review in reviews_data]
token_length_stats = pd.Series(review_token_length).describe()
token_length_stats
```
Since the mean number of tokens per review is 235 and roughly 75% of reviews are less then 286 tokens, a pad length of 300 is chosen.

```{python}
from sentiment_analysis.stats import fraction_word_coverage_distribution, vocab_coverage_needed
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

cumulative, counter  = fraction_word_coverage_distribution(texts = x_train) 
print(f"Total number of unique words in the input texts is: {len(counter)}")

print("The cummulative token distribution indicates that most of the reviews have common words.")

def plot_cumulative_coverage(cumulative_distribution: list[float]):
  # 1. Setup figure
  fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5), dpi=100)
    
    # 2. X-axis tracking (word count ranking)
  num_words = np.arange(1, len(cumulative_distribution) + 1)
    
    # 3. Simple line plot
  ax.plot(num_words, cumulative_distribution, color="#1a365d", linewidth=2)
    
    # 4. Titles and labels
  ax.set_title("Cumulative Token Coverage Distribution", fontsize=12, weight="bold", pad=10)
  ax.set_xlabel("Number of Unique Words", fontsize=10)
  ax.set_ylabel("Fraction of Total Tokens", fontsize=10)
    
    # 5. Clean layout adjustments
  ax.set_ylim(0, 1.05)
  ax.set_xlim(0, len(num_words))
  ax.grid(True, linestyle=":", alpha=0.5)
    
    # Remove top and right borders for a cleaner look
  for spine in ["top", "right"]:
    ax.spines[spine].set_visible(False)
        
  plt.tight_layout()
  plt.show()

plot_cumulative_coverage(cumulative_distribution=cumulative)

print("Here is a list of most common words and the number of times they occur in the vocabulary")

top_10_word_and_counts = counter.most_common(10)

df_top_words = pd.DataFrame(top_10_word_and_counts, columns=["Word","Frequency"])
#df_top_words.style.hide(axis='index')
gt_top_words = GT(df_top_words)
gt_top_words
```

```{python}
print("To enable efficient running of the LSTM model, it is necessary to restrict the vocab to certain set of unique words only")
print("Here is a table of number of unique words vs. the coverage range")

t_90 = vocab_coverage_needed(cummulative_distribution=cumulative, threshold=.90)
t_95 = vocab_coverage_needed(cummulative_distribution=cumulative, threshold=.95)
t_98 = vocab_coverage_needed(cummulative_distribution=cumulative, threshold=.98)

vocab_coverage = [("90%",t_90),("95%",t_95),("98%",t_98)]
df_vocab_coverage = pd.DataFrame(vocab_coverage, columns=["Coverage(%)","Unique words needed"])
gt_vocab_coverage = GT(df_vocab_coverage)
gt_vocab_coverage
```

# Encoding and Tensor creation

## Encoding 

The datasets are encoded. Here is an example of an encoded review as a numpy array!

```{python}
from sentiment_analysis.vocab_and_encoding import encode_train_text_val_dataset

x_train_encoded, x_val_encoded, x_test_encoded = encode_train_text_val_dataset(
    x_train_data=x_train,x_val_data=x_val,x_test_data=x_test
)
first_review_encoded = np.array(x_train_encoded[0])

print(f"Numpy array of an encoded review: {first_review_encoded}")
```
The review was shorter than 300 tokens, so the trailing numbers are all zeroes. 

## Tensors

Batch size = 32;

Instead of feeding all 25,000 reviews to the model at once (which would blow up the memory and give noisy/slow gradient updates), the DataLoader splits the dataset into chunks of 32 examples each. shuffle randomises the list.

train_loader = DataLoader(train_dataset,batch_size=32,shuffle=True)

val_loader = DataLoader(val_dataset,batch_size=32, shuffle=True)

test_loader = DataLoader(test_dataset, batch_size=32, shuffle = True)

```{python}
import torch
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader, TensorDataset
device = torch.device("mps" if torch.mps.is_available() else "cpu")

y_train = np.array([1 if y == "positive" else 0 for y in y_train])
y_val = np.array([1 if y=="positive" else 0 for y in y_val])
y_test = np.array([1 if y=="positive" else 0 for y in y_test])

X_train_tensor = torch.tensor(x_train_encoded, dtype=torch.long, device=device)
y_train_tensor = torch.tensor(y_train, dtype=torch.float, device=device)

X_val_tensor = torch.tensor(x_val_encoded, dtype=torch.long, device=device)
y_val_tensor = torch.tensor(y_val, dtype=torch.float, device=device)

X_test_tensor = torch.tensor(x_test_encoded, dtype=torch.long, device=device)
y_test_tensor = torch.tensor(y_test, dtype=torch.float, device=device)

    # TensorDataset wraps X and y tensors together so that indexing returns matched (input,label)
train_dataset = TensorDataset(X_train_tensor,y_train_tensor)
val_dataset = TensorDataset(X_val_tensor,y_val_tensor)
test_dataset = TensorDataset(X_test_tensor,y_test_tensor)

# Creating batches using Dataloader (batch size = 32)

batch_size = 32

train_loader = DataLoader(train_dataset,batch_size,shuffle=True)

val_loader = DataLoader(val_dataset,batch_size, shuffle=True)

test_loader = DataLoader(test_dataset, batch_size, shuffle = True)

xb , yb = next(iter(train_loader))
print(f"The shape of an X_tensor is: {xb.shape}")
print(f"The shape of an y tensor is: {yb.shape}")
```
